Thirteen comments

An old and famous piping jig. Maybe its simplicity can deceive the player; It seems to be a monotonous tune, and therefore easy to play, but I think that all those rolls are quite tricky and should be played very carefully, you know, to give the feeling that there are exactly 3 notes played in a row etc. So I suppose it’s not as simple as it might sound.

The reason why I love this tune so much is its dramatic character. The melody moves heavily around the same chord, most of the time, and everything is done with the lowest notes of our virtual uilleann pipes’ chanter. Just imagine the drones in the background… hmmm. beautifully irritating, I think.

↳ Posted by Netallica on September 26th, 2002.

Oh yes!

thanks for posting this one! it’s one of my favourites and i cpould hear played a LOT of times round.
i first listened to this on the Paddy Glackin album ‘in full spate’ where he plays it after ‘i burried my wife’ with Robbie Hannon.
it’s a driver and a belter.

↳ Posted by biggus dave on September 26th, 2002.

From the sleeve notes of The Pipering of Willie Clancy Vol. II:

“Willie had a special regard for this tune. Fraher, a piper who was born around 1800, passed the tune on to James Burke. His pupil the Reverend Brother Gildas gave it to Willie.”

↳ Posted by CreadurMawnOrganig on September 27th, 2002.

Fraher’s, X:13

I’ve got this haunting tune long long ago when listening to “Doublin’ ”, the great album by Paddy Keenan & Paddy Glackin . Thanks again to them about 40 years later ;) I’ve done my best here to be close to the setting of their first playing according to
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5wORhW_b4QE (it start at 1mn 31).
Technical detail : this tool seems not precise enough to write ornementations on the score ; it is a cran for low D and a common roll for A (see the book about Willie Clancy’s music for details).
Also it is pretty close of setting #10 by UPipes & harp . Thanks to her/him.
